clue.text: Two drinks, one behind another

parts.note: the first drink is a sup, a mouthful of liquid
the second drink is porter, a dark beer

explanation.surface: A pair of glasses lined up on the bar, one in the queue after the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one behind another' seems to describe how the drinks are arranged, but it is the definition: a person who stands behind someone else, backing them.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic sense: to be behind someone is to back them, so a backer is one person behind another.

clue.text: Go around capital of Italy — as it used to be

definitions.text: Go around capital of Italy — as it used to be

indicators.note: around tells you the word for go wraps round the letter that follows

parts.note: a go is a turn, as in a board game

indicators.note: capital of points to the opening letter of the word Italy

explanation.surface: A suggestion to tour the city that was once the seat of Italian government.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: this city was the first capital of unified Italy, from 1861 to 1865, before Florence and then Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Historical fact: the Piedmontese city was the first seat of government of the unified kingdom in 1861.

clue.text: Drug horse that's backed with foreign agreement

indicators.note: backed tells you the word for horse is written from its last letter to its first

parts.note: a nag is an old or worn-out horse
ja is yes in German, an agreement in a foreign tongue

explanation.surface: A doped racehorse has been wagered on under some overseas deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's backed' turns NAG into GAN; in the surface it reads as a horse someone has bet on. 'Horse' is also slang for heroin, a neat false trail beside 'Drug'.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang name for cannabis, which is a narcotic.

clue.text: Ultimately dumb, clear?

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word dumb

parts.note: a clear day or sky is a rainless one, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is plain that a person is as stupid as can be.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue serves as the definition as well as the wordplay: someone ultimately dumb is as stupid as it gets.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for utterly stupid, which is what being dumb in the extreme amounts to.

clue.text: Artist has European city university in streaky claret

parts.note: Toulouse is a city in south-west France

indicators.note: in places the letter for university inside the rearranged wine
streaky suggests something smeared and run together, so the letters of claret are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter is linked with a continental college town and a smeared spill of red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'streaky' rearranges CLARET into LATREC, and 'in' puts U inside it to give LAUTREC. The link word 'has' joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was the French painter of Parisian nightlife and Moulin Rouge posters.

clue.text: Innkeeper to catch supposed drunkard?

parts.note: to land a fish is to catch it
the saying 'drunk as a lord' supposes that a peer is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A publican sets out to nab someone he thinks has had too many.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supposed drunkard' relies on the British simile 'drunk as a lord'; the question mark admits the cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the person who runs a pub or inn is called this, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Tissue died within part of joint

indicators.note: within places the letter for died inside the word for part of a joint

parts.note: a tenon is the projecting piece of a mortise-and-tenon woodworking joint
D is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A medical report says the flesh inside part of a knee or elbow has perished.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'joint' looks anatomical beside 'Tissue', but it is a carpenter's joint; 'within' puts D inside TENON.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an example of connective tissue, the cord attaching muscle to bone.

clue.text: Work of art heading for exhibition in museum, not initialled

indicators.note: in places the letter from exhibition inside the shortened museum
not initialled means the museum's name goes without its initial letter

parts.note: the Louvre is the great art museum in Paris

indicators.note: heading for points to the opening letter of the word exhibition

explanation.surface: A painting bound for a gallery show has not been signed off with initials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not initialled' strips the L from LOUVRE to leave OUVRE, and 'in' puts E inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word means an artistic or literary work, or an artist's whole output.

clue.text: Hot flower, blue for the ladies, perhaps?

parts.note: lava is molten rock that flows, so it is a hot thing that flows, a 'flow-er'
blue is the colour of the Conservative Party in Britain, whose members are Tories

explanation.surface: A warm-coloured bloom, or perhaps a cooler shade, chosen as a gift for the women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' wants to be a bloom; it is something that flows. 'The ladies' is British for a women's public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: The ladies is a euphemism for a women's toilet, one example of the room in question.

clue.text: Old man taking nap with the courtship, sadly

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters before it are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly gent regrettably dozes off in the middle of wooing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges NAP, THE and COURTSHIP together. 'Old man' is not an elderly chap but an early human.
explanation.definitionFit: The former genus name of Java Man, a prehistoric hominid, so a very ancient human.

clue.text: Possible replacement for a top state

definitions.meaning: a top is a garment for the upper body; in Britain a pullover is a jersey, and a fresh one could replace an old top
one of the United States, on the Atlantic coast next to New York

explanation.definitionFit: A fresh pullover could stand in for a worn-out top, and the same two words name an American state.

clue.text: Financier losing unspecified amount is one making a bloomer?

indicators.note: losing tells you the financier gives up the letter that follows

parts.note: a banker is a financier
N stands for an unspecified number in mathematics

explanation.surface: A money man who drops an undisclosed sum is the sort to make a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is British slang for a blunder, but also a crusty loaf with diagonal slashes; the definition uses the loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a kind of British loaf, so the person making one works with dough and an oven.

clue.text: Home fit for rats — you stitching me up?

definitions.meaning: an underground drain for waste, where rats live
a person using needle and thread on a garment is one who sews

explanation.definitionFit: An underground drain is where rats thrive, and the same spelling names a person working with needle and thread.

clue.text: Thrilling descent as current swirls

indicators.note: swirls describes things whirling about, so the letters before it are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exciting ride down a river as the water eddies round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swirls' rearranges AS and CURRENT together. The answer is the famous ice toboggan track at St Moritz in Switzerland.
explanation.definitionFit: The St Moritz skeleton toboggan track, an example of an exciting downhill ride.

clue.text: Faculty's reference for the audience

definitions.note: the 's is only a link; a faculty is one of the senses

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word for reference is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to reference a source is to cite it

explanation.surface: A university department's letter of recommendation is read out to those assembled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' looks like a university department; it is one of the five senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A faculty is a power of mind or body, and vision is one of them.

clue.text: Formal wear for a king or emperor?

definitions.text: Formal wear for a king or emperor?

parts.words: Formal wear for a king or emperor?
parts.note: king and emperor are not monarchs here but two species of a black-and-white flightless bird, whose colouring gives a man's dinner jacket its nickname

explanation.surface: Ceremonial clothes fit for a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a man's black-and-white evening dress, named after the birds it resembles.

clue.text: Experiencing success after success — like butter, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: an idiom for enjoying a winning streak
where butter is often found: spread upon a small round piece of bread

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a winning streak also describes, literally, where butter sits when spread upon a bun.

clue.text: Certainly true, so be curious

indicators.note: curious means odd or strange, so the three words before it are put in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: It is undoubtedly correct, therefore one should be inquisitive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curious' looks like an instruction to be inquisitive, but it rearranges TRUE, SO and BE.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase of agreement meaning undoubtedly or of course.

clue.text: Are you kidding, exceptionally?

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of disbelief, asked as a one-word question
an intensifier meaning very or extremely

explanation.definitionFit: As a question the word expresses disbelief, and as an adverb it is an intensifier meaning extremely.

clue.text: Heavy weight certain to make severe cut on head

parts.note: a ton is a heavy unit of weight
certain means sure

explanation.surface: A massive object is bound to cause a nasty scalp wound.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'cut' is not a wound but a haircut: the shaved crown of a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk's shaved crown is a drastic haircut on the top of the scalp.

clue.text: Cry over philanderer ditching love

indicators.note: ditching tells you the philanderer throws away the letter for love

parts.note: a roué is a dissolute man, a womaniser
love is a score of nothing in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: Someone weeps about a womaniser who has dumped his sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' is part of the definition, not a signal to turn anything round.
explanation.definitionFit: To regret something bitterly is to weep about it, as with spilt milk.

clue.text: Snow in no little time, with February's end

parts.note: a sec is a short moment, short for second
with means and, as in 'fish with chips'

indicators.note: end points to the final letter of February, the possessive s aside

explanation.surface: A blizzard arrives very quickly as winter's shortest month closes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snow' is not the weather but slang for cocaine, as is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang terms for cocaine, a powder taken by sniffing.

clue.text: One bedded in passionate game

parts.note: red-hot describes intense passion
poker is a card game

explanation.surface: Somebody taken to bed during an ardent bit of sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One bedded' is a plant set in a flower bed: the answer is the garden plant kniphofia, with flame-coloured flower spikes.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden perennial with fiery spikes, something planted in a flower border.

clue.text: Many clothes on youthful boy, seventies fashion?

indicators.note: as a verb, clothes means wraps round, so the word for many goes round what follows

parts.note: lots means many
Peter Pan is the boy who never grew up

explanation.surface: A lad wearing layer upon layer of garments in the style of forty years back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' reads as a plural noun for garments, but it is a verb meaning wraps round. The answer is the British name for the widely flared trousers of the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: Widely flared trousers that were a popular style in that decade.

clue.text: Am tetchy when relocating plant

indicators.note: relocating means moving to new positions, so the letters before it change places

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener admits to being irritable while moving a shrub to a new spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when relocating' rearranges AM and TETCHY together.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind of germander, an aromatic Mediterranean herb that cats love, so an example of the category.

clue.text: "Say, take us back to shore, darling, to see Bambi?"

indicators.note: say tells you the request that follows is spoken, and its sound is what matters

parts.words: take us back to shore, darling
parts.note: someone in a boat asking a loved one to get back to land would say 'Row, dear'

explanation.surface: A request to a sweetheart to turn the boat round so they can watch a famous fawn.
explanation.walkthrough: In Felix Salten's original novel Bambi belongs to this small European species, hence the question mark for a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambi, in the original Austrian novel, is an example of this small woodland species.

clue.text: A Balkan kidnapping bishop — one taking a tumble?

indicators.note: a kidnapper seizes and holds someone, so the Balkan person holds the bishop's letter inside

parts.note: a Croat is a person from Croatia, in the Balkans
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A man from south-east Europe abducts a clergyman, and someone falls over in the struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking a tumble' suggests an accident; here tumbling is the performer's skill.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnastic performer whose act includes tumbling, so the fall is deliberate.

clue.text: Dissect speed of light as a measure of astronomy

parts.note: to parse a sentence is to take it apart into its components
c is the symbol for the speed of light in physics, as in E = mc squared

explanation.surface: A scientist takes apart the velocity of light as a yardstick for studying the stars.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of distance used by astronomers, about 3.26 light years.

clue.text: Father Brown's ultimate charmer

parts.note: to sire is to father offspring, and a sire is a male parent

indicators.note: ultimate points to the final letter of Brown, the possessive s aside

explanation.surface: G. K. Chesterton's priest detective turns out to be thoroughly delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Brown is Chesterton's fictional priest-detective; the two words must be split, 'Father' alone giving SIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A seductive enchantress, like the mythical singers who lured sailors.

clue.text: However you look at it, that's incredible!

indicators.note: whichever direction you read it from, the word is spelt the same

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: From any angle, the thing is simply unbelievable.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of amazement, what one says at something astonishing.
